lesson.title: Motive, Phrase and Period
lesson.summary: Motives grow into phrases, phrases end with cadences, and pairs of phrases form periods and sentences.

section.title: Motive
section.p: A motive is the smallest recognisable musical idea: a short group of notes with a characteristic rhythm, contour or both. Composers build longer passages by repeating and varying motives:

list.li: Sequence: the motive repeated at a higher or lower pitch level.
Inversion: the motive with its directions turned upside down.
Augmentation and diminution: the motive in longer or shorter note values.
Fragmentation: only a part of the motive, repeated or developed.

figure.staff: C5/e D5/e E5/q | D5/e E5/e F5/q | C5/e B4/e A4/q | C5/q D5/q | E5/h |.
figure.caption: A motive of three rising notes, its sequence a step higher, its inversion, and its augmentation in notes twice as long.

section.p: The inversion above keeps the steps but not their exact sizes: within the key, a rising whole step can become a falling half step. This is called a diatonic inversion.

check.prompt: A motive is repeated starting a step higher, with the same rhythm and contour. What is this called?
check.explanation: Repeating a motive at another pitch level is a sequence. An inversion turns its directions upside down, and augmentation lengthens its note values.

section.title: Phrase
section.p: A phrase is a complete musical thought that ends with a cadence. Phrases are often four bars long, but two, three, five or eight bars are possible too; what defines a phrase is its cadence, not its length. This is the definition of Kostka and Payne and most American textbooks; Caplin uses the word more loosely, for a unit of about four bars whether or not it ends with a cadence.

Listen for where the music comes to rest: a phrase ending on V, with a half cadence, sounds like a question, and one ending on I with a perfect authentic cadence sounds like an answer. A phrase is often divided into shorter subphrases, but without its own cadence a unit is not a phrase.

check.prompt: What defines the end of a phrase?
check.explanation: A phrase is a musical thought that ends with a cadence. Many phrases are four bars long and many end with a longer note or a rest, but neither makes a phrase.

section.title: Period: antecedent and consequent
section.p: A period is a pair of phrases in which the second answers the first. The first phrase, the antecedent, ends with a weaker cadence, usually a half cadence or an imperfect authentic cadence. The second phrase, the consequent, ends with a stronger cadence, usually a perfect authentic cadence.

figure.staff: E5/q C5/q G4/q C5/q | D5/q F5/q E5/q D5/q | C5/q E5/q A5/q F5/q | E5/h D5/h ||
figure.caption: The antecedent of a parallel period in C major: four bars ending with a half cadence on V.

figure.staff: E5/q C5/q G4/q C5/q | D5/q F5/q E5/q D5/q | C5/q E5/q A5/q F5/q | E5/q D5/q C5/h |.
C3/w | B2/w | C3/h F2/h | G2/h C3/h |.
figure.caption: The consequent: it begins like the antecedent and ends with a perfect authentic cadence.

section.p: When the two phrases begin with the same or similar music, the period is a parallel period; when they begin differently, it is a contrasting period. If both phrases end with the same cadence, the second does not answer the first, and most textbooks call the pair a repeated phrase or a phrase group rather than a period.

check.prompt: Which cadence typically ends the antecedent of a period?
check.option: A deceptive cadence followed by a plagal cadence
check.explanation: The antecedent ends with a weaker cadence, most often a half cadence, so that the consequent can answer it with a stronger one, usually a perfect authentic cadence.

check.prompt: Two phrases begin with the same melody; the first ends on V and the second on I with a perfect authentic cadence. What is the form?
check.explanation: The second phrase answers the first with a stronger cadence, so the pair is a period, and because both phrases begin alike it is a parallel period. A repeated phrase would end both times with the same cadence.

section.title: Sentence
section.p: The sentence is another common eight-bar theme, described by Arnold Schoenberg and in detail by William Caplin. It has two halves of four bars:

list.li: The presentation: a two-bar basic idea, then its repetition, exact or on another harmony, often the dominant.
The continuation: shorter fragments of the idea, often with faster harmonic rhythm or a sequence, leading to a cadence.

figure.staff: D5/q B4/q G4/q B4/q | C5/q A4/q F#4/h | C5/q A4/q F#4/q A4/q | B4/q G4/q G4/h ||
figure.caption: The presentation of a sentence in G major: the basic idea over I–V7, then its repetition over V7–I.

figure.staff: E5/q C5/q D5/q B4/q | C5/q A4/q E5/q C5/q | B4/q D5/q C5/q A4/q | G4/w |.
C3/h B2/h | A2/h C3/h | D3/w | G2/w |.
figure.caption: The continuation: two-note fragments with a chord every two beats, then a perfect authentic cadence.

section.p: Not every textbook uses the term: many North American harmony texts describe themes mainly as periods. The two forms differ in their middles: a period cadences after four bars, a sentence does not.

check.prompt: What happens in the first four bars of a sentence?
check.option: A phrase ending with a half cadence
A two-bar basic idea and its repetition
check.explanation: The presentation states a basic idea and repeats it, without a cadence. The fragments and the cadence come in the continuation; a half cadence after four bars belongs to a period.
